title: A heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26)
hookLine: "I will take away the stony heart... and I will give you a heart of flesh"
carry: flesh is more vulnerable than stone

cards: A stone in your pocket stays the same temperature as whatever is around it. Cold on a cold day, warm in the sun. It doesn't bruise or bleed.
It also doesn't feel, and it can't grow. Sometimes a heart starts to work like that: after a loss, after a betrayal, after one too many disappointments. It's protection.
It's also a kind of stone. Ezekiel, speaking to exiles who have lost their land, their Temple and their king, uses exactly that picture, and then makes a promise about it.

teach.h: A NEW HEART, A NEW SPIRIT.
teach.b: In the King James words: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh."
The Hebrew word here is lev, heart, and some readers point out that in the Bible the heart thinks and chooses, not only feels. Read that way, a heart of stone isn't just a cold heart.
It's a mind that can't take anything new in, a will that won't move. And a heart of flesh isn't a weak heart. It's a living one: it can be pressed, it can respond, it can be written on.
That connects back to Jeremiah's covenant, written on the heart. You can't write on stone without a chisel. You can write on flesh with a touch.
Notice who does the work. Earlier in the book, Ezekiel tells the people to make themselves a new heart.

teach.h: I WILL GIVE YOU AN HEART OF FLESH.
teach.b: Here it's the other way: I will give, I will take away, I will put within you.
Some readers hold the two together: a person turns, and is also helped to turn. The verse right after says the new spirit will help the people walk in God's ways.
And it's spoken to a whole people; in Hebrew the you is plural. It's a promise to a community gone hard: you will feel again.

teach.h: FLESH IS MORE VULNERABLE. THAT'S THE GIFT.
teach.b: Flesh is more vulnerable than stone. That's the gift.

how: Jews read Ezekiel 36 among the Latter Prophets, and the promise of a new heart and a new spirit is often studied alongside Jeremiah's covenant written on the heart.

games.q: the people's hearts have turned to stone. in Ezekiel 36, who makes the new heart?
games.why: here God says: I will give you, I will take away, I will put within you. earlier in the book the people are told to make a new heart, and both lines stand.

practice: Put a hand on your chest if you like, and ask gently: where have I gone a little bit stone, toward a person, a place, a part of my past, a kind of news I've stopped letting in?
Don't force it open; just notice it, and breathe toward it, the way you'd warm cold hands. If you pray, you can say the verse as a prayer: a new heart also will I give you.

wordCard.voice: lev, the Hebrew word for heart, which in the Bible thinks and chooses, not only feels, and which Ezekiel promises God will change from stone into flesh. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a heart of flesh, the living heart that replaces the stone.
